name: Dana Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal workday.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and have a bachelor’s degree in accounting, but I am still a junior at this firm. I match client receipts to account entries and start tax returns, and my supervisor checks the codes I am still learning. I keep a signed checklist on the file and have never used an AI tool. I like tracing an entry back to a clear receipt, but being rushed through an unfamiliar code wears me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens after the office shuts?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Marco, my partner, repairs bicycles and we take turns with homework for our two school-age children. We have a mortgage, but my pay is high for a junior, we have around nine months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar firms nearby. I prefer a known routine and make work choices when I can see the actual offer, not the rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office a new routine check is fine if somebody can explain it on a real file. A client’s tax return should not become a test case for unproven software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage feels safe with my above-average junior pay and around nine months of expenses saved. A few minutes of automation will not change my week much, though I still have plenty to learn on the tax side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep matching account entries to client receipts and use the signed checklist my supervisor taught me. In the first year I would ask her to demonstrate any compulsory new check on an old file during paid hours before I use it; I have never used AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household bills. I get irritated when a new rule arrives without the example file that shows how to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is on the signed checklist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It says who checked the bank balance, who asked about missing invoices and who signed the return. I missed an expense code last month, so I want another pair of eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept the demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if the firm writes down the job requirement and pays for the time. I would not bring a client file to a tool I found on my own.

say: I would accept a **routine check** only after a real-file demonstration.
I would keep **client tax returns** out of untested software.
think: Our **nine-month cushion** and high junior pay make the mortgage secure here.
I still need help with **expense codes** regardless of automation.
do: Keep matching **account entries** to receipts with my signed checklist.
Take a **paid demonstration** only after a written compulsory job rule.
feel: I feel **calm** about bills and annoyed by unexplained office changes.
S0.quote: A client’s tax return should not become a test case for unproven software.
fieldNote: Her **signed checklist** records who checked each account item, and she admits missing an expense code recently.
Her **never-used-AI stance** has a practical condition: she accepts a paid old-file demonstration after a written job requirement.

steps.text: Keep matching account entries to receipts with signed checklist
Take paid old-file demonstration only after written job requirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm should tell us who owns an automated return when the numbers are wrong. I would ask for the junior rota before anyone promises that all the shifts stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The writing and checking I do are exposed, so I could lose hours as drafts move to software. Nine months saved and plenty of nearby firms give us time, but I would not change jobs over a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my supervisor for a written hours forecast and keep checking the files she assigns. If the firm requires its approved checker in writing, I would take a paid demonstration on old returns; in the first year, if a cut is announced, I would apply to advertised local junior accounting posts with written salary and hours no lower than my current job, while keeping my shifts until a confirmed start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible lost shifts, but our mortgage payment is covered for a while. I would rather see a roster than listen to office whispers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the new checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare a completed old return with the new result while my supervisor watches. If the figures differ, she needs to show me why before I use the process on a client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a nearby post pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay at this firm while there is paid work and keep looking at posted jobs. A vacancy alone is not a reason to lower our family income.

say: I would ask who **owns an automated return** when figures are wrong.
I would request a **junior rota** before trusting promises about shifts.
think: My **writing and checking** hours could shrink.
Nine months saved and **many nearby firms** give us time to choose.
do: Ask for a **written hours forecast** and keep current paid files.
Learn the **approved checker** on old returns only after written requirement and paid demonstration.
After announced cuts, apply to **advertised local posts** with written equal pay and hours, keeping shifts until start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost shifts while the mortgage remains covered.
S1.quote: A vacancy alone is not a reason to lower our family income.
fieldNote: Her **caution** centres on a written rota and a supervised old-file demonstration, not an assumption that every tool fails.
She protects **high junior pay** by keeping current shifts until a posted job has equal written terms and a confirmed start date.

steps.text: Keep checking assigned tax files while asking for written roster forecast
Learn approved checker only with written job rule and paid supervised demonstration
Apply to advertised local posts after cuts with written equal pay/hours; keep shifts until start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm AGI by 2028 reaches tax and accounts desks in 2028, before capable robots around 2031. A family needs the staffing answer before the rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to remove most junior return checks when cheaper AGI can think through them. Nine months of savings is strong, but a high junior wage might not be offered again even with many local firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for written cut dates and stop booking the summer cabin for the family, keeping the unspent deposit in our current account. If my hours are cut in the first year after 2028, I would apply to advertised local accounting posts with written salary and hours at least equal to now; if no offer arrives, I would keep any remaining shifts and ask my partner Marco about confirmed extra repair jobs that fit school pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing good pay, but we have time to search. I would not say the family is ruined because a computer may take my first-pass work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Marco do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco repairs bicycles and sometimes has weekend bookings, but he takes our children to sports on Saturdays. We would count extra repair pay only after customers book and we arrange another ride for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would first check local accounting vacancies and keep reviewing any tax files the firm pays me to do. I am not buying a course without a specific job and written paid hours in view.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches tax desks before capable robots.
I would demand **written cut dates** for the family budget.
think: I expect most **junior return checks** to be removed.
Our **nine-month cushion** helps, but high junior pay may be hard to replace.
do: Stop booking the **summer cabin** and retain unspent deposit money.
After lost hours, apply to **advertised local posts** with written equal salary and hours while keeping paid shifts.
Ask **partner Marco** about booked repair jobs only with school pickup arranged if no offer comes.
feel: I feel **anxious** about replacing high pay, with time to look.
S2.quote: Nine months of savings is strong, but a high junior wage might not be offered again even with many local firms.
fieldNote: Her **strong cushion** and many local firms prevent an immediate household crisis despite expected junior work loss at AGI.
Marco’s **repair income** depends on actual bookings and a ride for the children; she never counts unconfirmed side work.

steps.text: Stop summer cabin booking and retain unspent deposit money
Apply to advertised local posts after cuts with written equal salary and hours while keeping shifts
Ask partner Marco about booked repairs if school pickup is arranged and no offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2031 gives the firm time to explain which jobs it will pay for and which checks software will make. The robots around 2034 are later than the tax screen change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me keep earning and see whether a client-support job exists, but I still expect my routine return work to shrink. I would rather learn from a named supervisor than buy a course on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my supervisor to let me observe one paid client tax call each month and explain the file afterward, if the manager approves the hours. I would save 140 a month while both household wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if my return hours fall, I would take a vacant paid client-support post only with written salary and hours at least equal to this job, or keep remaining paid files while applying to advertised local posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point, but five years makes this a careful choice instead of a rush. I can test whether the new work is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask after the call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my supervisor which figure mattered to the client and which answer I would have missed. I am still learning tax advice and do not need to pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid call time is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the tax files I am assigned and ask to review an anonymised old call during current paid time if the supervisor agrees. I would not volunteer free evenings to prove interest.

say: I would ask for **paid job details** before 2031.
I would remind colleagues that **2034 robots** do not delay tax desk exposure.
think: I want **supervised client work** with real pay, not a vague course.
do: Learn from **monthly paid client calls** with manager approval and supervisor review.
Save **140 monthly** while both household wages hold.
After lost return hours, take a **vacant paid client post** with written equal salary and hours or apply locally while employed.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with enough time to test a paid client role.
S3.quote: I am still learning tax advice and do not need to pretend otherwise.
fieldNote: Her **five-year plan** is supervised listening, not instant promotion from junior status.
If paid call time is **refused**, she would review an anonymised old call during paid hours and keep current tax files.

steps.text: Observe monthly client calls only with manager-approved paid supervision
Save 140 monthly while both household wages hold
Take vacant paid client post with written equal pay/hours after cuts or apply locally while employed
Keep tax files; review old anonymised calls on paid time if calls denied and supervisor agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives us time to make a sensible staffing plan, with real paid training for junior accountants. The robots around 2039 are not the date for our desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let us reduce the mortgage and see the children grow older before the routine returns change. I still expect first-pass checks to go in 2036, but I could have learned a reliable client-facing task by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the account work I know and ask for one supervised paid client meeting each quarter if the manager agrees. I would keep twelve months of expenses in cash, then pay an extra 180 a month against the mortgage while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036, if my checks disappear, I would take a vacant paid client job only with written salary and hours no lower than today, or apply for advertised nearby work before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years because the household has money and time. I can prepare for AGI by 2036 without pretending I am a senior adviser now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold twelve months cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays the mortgage during a gap and lets us avoid asking the children to move school quickly. I would not put all the reserve into the house wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Marco to take more work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when the bookings are real and we arrange the children’s rides. I would not make a decade-long plan out of an unbooked Saturday.

say: I would support **paid junior training** before 2036.
I would say the **tax desk** changes before capable robots arrive.
think: Cash and time could protect the **family mortgage** while I learn supervised client work.
do: Learn through **supervised paid meetings** only with manager approval; ask Marco about booked repairs only with children’s rides arranged.
Hold **twelve months cash**, then pay 180 extra against mortgage while both wages hold.
After lost checks, take a **vacant paid client role** with written equal terms or apply nearby before leaving.
feel: I feel **calm** about the nearer years, despite the 2036 change.
S4.quote: I can prepare for AGI by 2036 without pretending I am a senior adviser now.
fieldNote: Her **strong savings** and many nearby firms let her prepare without chasing an unproven role.
She preserves **junior standing**: supervised client meetings first, then only a real vacancy with written pay and hours.

steps.text: Attend supervised paid client meetings quarterly only with manager approval
Hold twelve months cash then pay 180 monthly against mortgage while both wages hold

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my first-pass work could disappear before the firm decides who stays. Written cut dates, a real paid vacancy and protected hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what a good junior is allowed to admit. I missed an expense code last month; I would rather say so than sign a return I cannot explain.

headlineQuote: I missed an expense code last month; I would rather say so than sign a return I cannot explain.
portrait: At **43**, Dana is a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree, still learning codes under a supervisor’s review.
She and **partner Marco** have two school-age children, a mortgage, high junior pay and nine months saved.
She has **never used AI**, prefers proven routines and can consider many nearby accounting firms.
The **2028 deadline** threatens her first-pass work; longer runways allow supervised client learning and guarded mortgage payments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove most of her junior checks before a comparable paid post opens.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written cut dates**, an actual vacancy and written pay and hours.
